query: Equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr exhibits 8–16% room-temperature tensile ductility in the cast state and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C at strain rates of 10−4–10−2 s−1, but inadequate oxygen resistance prevents most practical high-temperature applications. Earlier oxidation-protection research prevented pesting in a related, non-equiatomic Hf–Nb–Ta–Ti–Zr alloy during a 5 h exposure to air at 800 °C, but that result does not establish protection for equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr; related studies on other refractory alloys likewise did not evaluate this composition. With preservation of useful room- and high-temperature mechanical performance as a design constraint, what single intervention could improve the oxygen resistance of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr? Formulate one hypothesis identifying the intervention and mechanism, predicting the outcome relative to untreated material, defining the applicable temperature, atmosphere, exposure-time, and loading boundaries, citing supporting evidence from the prior studies, and specifying a controlled experiment and result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A thin, diffusion‐bonded silicide coating (specifically a Si–20Cr–20Fe layer) applied to cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr will form a protective, continuous silicide/oxide scale during high‐temperature exposure that significantly reduces oxygen uptake (and hence pesting) without degrading its room‐ and high‐temperature mechanical performance.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr exhibiting 8–16% room‐temperature tensile ductility and a yield strength of 163–530 MPa at 1000 °C, but showing inadequate oxygen resistance in air.
generation.intervention: Deposit a thin Si–20Cr–20Fe silicide coating by a fused slurry method followed by a high‐temperature heat treatment (e.g., ~1430 °C for 1 h in low‐pressure/controlled atmosphere) to promote interfacial diffusion and in situ formation of silicide phases.
generation.conditions: Exposure in static air at 1000 °C for 5 hours; maintaining the original microstructure so that tensile tests at room temperature and at 1000 °C can be compared to untreated material.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a dual-layer silicide structure (an outer high-silicon MSi2 layer and an inner lower-silicon M5Si3 layer) that, upon oxidation, converts into a dense, adherent oxide scale which acts as an oxygen diffusion barrier.
generation.mechanism: The silicide coating reacts during high-temperature exposure to form a protective oxide (comprising, for example, silica and mixed-metal oxides) that significantly slows oxygen ingress. This barrier minimizes pesting and oxidation without altering the beneficial bulk mechanical properties of the HfNbTaTiZr alloy.
generation.predicted_outcome: A significant reduction in mass gain (and by inference, oxidation rate) during high-temperature exposure relative to the untreated cast alloy, while room-temperature ductility and high-temperature yield strength remain within an acceptable range compared to the baseline.
generation.baseline: Untreated equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr exhibits rapid oxidation (e.g., exponential kinetics with high mass gain) under similar conditions and suffers from poor oxygen resistance despite its useful mechanical performance.
generation.boundary: Applicable under high-temperature static air exposure conditions of approximately 1000 °C for durations up to 5 hours, with the requirement that the intervention does not alter the bulk microstructure or degrade tensile properties at room and elevated temperatures.
generation.uncertainty: The long-term adhesion of the silicide coating and potential interdiffusion effects at the coating/substrate interface remain uncertain, as does the scalability of the coating process without inducing residual stresses or microstructural degradation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of equiatomic cast HfNbTaTiZr samples: one set with the Si–20Cr–20Fe coating (applied via the fused slurry method and appropriate heat treatment) and one uncoated control. Expose both sets to static air at 1000 °C for 5 hours. After exposure, assess oxide scale formation via microscopy and measure mass gain. Additionally, perform tensile tests at room temperature and at 1000 °C on both sets to evaluate any changes in mechanical performance.
measurements: Mass gain per unit area (mg/cm²) after oxidation test
Phase and microstructural analysis of the oxide scale (XRD/SEM/EDS)
Room-temperature tensile elongation and yield strength
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coated samples show a mass gain not significantly lower (i.e. within experimental error) than the uncoated baseline or if mechanical properties (ductility or yield strength) degrade by more than ~10% compared to the untreated samples, then the hypothesis that the coating improves oxygen resistance without compromising mechanical performance would be falsified.
